passages.t: Wine the mocker, and a heart no one can call pure
passages.happening:
‘Wine is a mocker, strong drink is a brawler, and whoever is led astray by them is not wise’ (verse 1). ‘The terror of a king is like the roar of a lion’ (verse 2). ‘It is honorable for a man to resolve a dispute, but any fool will quarrel’ (verse 3). ‘The slacker does not plow in season; at harvest time he looks, but nothing is there’ (verse 4).

‘The intentions of a man’s heart are deep waters, but a man of understanding draws them out’ (verse 5). ‘Many a man proclaims his loving devotion, but who can find a trustworthy man?’ (verse 6). ‘The righteous man walks with integrity; blessed are his children after him’ (verse 7). A king on his judgment seat sifts out evil with his eyes (verse 8).

Then a question that humbles every reader: no one can claim to have kept his heart pure, or to be clean from his sin (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Wine was a normal part of Israelite life and a sign of God's good gifts. Strong drink, shekar, probably meant beer or other fermented drinks. Proverbs does not forbid either. It warns vividly that they mock and brawl, and that whoever is led astray by them is not wise. A fuller warning comes in 23:29-35.

If drinking has become hard to control, you do not have to face it alone. Tell someone you trust, and reach out to a doctor or a recovery group near you. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

What runs through this chapter is humility about knowing oneself. The heart's intentions are deep waters (verse 5). Many people speak of their loyalty, but a trustworthy person is rare (verse 6). And no one can say his heart is pure (verse 9). The wise person here is not the one who has mastered himself. It is the one who knows how much of himself he cannot see, and trusts it to God.
passages.later: The psalm praises the good gift: ‘wine that gladdens the heart of man’ (Psalm 104:15). Ecclesiastes says what verse 9 asks: ‘Surely there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins’ (Ecclesiastes 7:20). And John says it plainly: ‘If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves’ (1 John 1:8). He adds the hope: ‘If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness’ (1 John 1:9).
passages.hard:
If no one can say his heart is pure (verse 9), who are the righteous that Proverbs keeps praising?

Proverbs uses ‘righteous’ in two ways that can seem to clash. It constantly sets the righteous against the wicked as two kinds of people. Yet verse 9 says no one is spotless.

The tension is real, but it is not a contradiction. In the Old Testament a righteous person is not a sinless person. It is someone whose life is turned toward God and his ways: who fears the LORD, deals honestly, confesses sin and turns from evil. David is remembered as a man after God's own heart, and Psalm 51, one of the Bible's great prayers of confession, is linked with him. Righteousness in this sense is the direction of a life, not a perfect record.

Christian theology adds another layer. The New Testament teaches that no one is righteous by his own performance (Romans 3:10), and that righteousness before God is received as a gift through faith in Christ. Those who receive it are called to live righteously, and that is where the practical wisdom of Proverbs comes in. Different traditions describe how the gift and the life fit together in different words. All agree that verse 9 rules out self-righteousness, and that the righteous of Proverbs are people who know they need mercy.
passages.asks: The chapter says the heart's depths are hard to see. Ask what in your own heart you have never let anyone, God included, draw out. And ask God, as the psalmist did, to create in you a clean heart.

passages.t: Unequal weights, the buyer's boast, and bread of fraud
passages.happening:
Differing weights and unequal measures are both detestable to the LORD (verse 10). Even a young man is known by what he does (verse 11). Ears that hear and eyes that see, the LORD made them both (verse 12). ‘Do not love sleep, or you will grow poor; open your eyes, and you will have plenty of food’ (verse 13).

Then a scene from the market. The buyer calls the goods worthless, ‘but on the way out, he gloats’ (verse 14). ‘There is an abundance of gold and rubies, but lips of knowledge are a rare treasure’ (verse 15).

‘Food gained by fraud is sweet to a man, but later his mouth is full of gravel’ (verse 17). ‘Set plans by consultation’ (verse 18). Avoid the gossip who reveals secrets (verse 19). ‘Whoever curses his father or mother, his lamp will be extinguished in deepest darkness’ (verse 20). And ‘An inheritance gained quickly will not be blessed in the end’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The buyer in verse 14 runs down the goods to lower the price, then walks off boasting of his bargain. The saying catches a small dishonesty everyone recognizes.

Verse 16 concerns collateral. A lender could take a garment as a pledge, though the law required a poor man's cloak to be returned by sunset because it was his only covering at night. The saying advises taking the garment of someone rash enough to guarantee a stranger's debt, since he is a poor risk.

Two sayings on unequal weights (verses 10 and 23) frame this part of the chapter, as 11:1 and 16:11 did earlier. The bread of fraud tastes sweet at first and then turns to gravel.

A lamp going out (verse 20) was a picture of a household coming to an end.
passages.later: The law protected the poor borrower: ‘If you take your neighbor’s cloak as collateral, return it to him by sunset’ (Exodus 22:26).
passages.asks: The buyer's small lie and the merchant's false weight are both detestable to the LORD. Ask where you shade the truth to get a better deal. And ask whether you are chasing anything quickly that the verse says will not be good in the end.

passages.t: Wait on the LORD, and the lamp that searches
passages.happening:
‘Wait on the LORD, and He will save you’ (verse 22), instead of setting out to pay back an evil yourself. Unequal weights are detestable to him (verse 23). “A man’s steps are from the LORD, so how can anyone understand his own way?” (verse 24). ‘It is a trap for a man to dedicate something rashly, only later to reconsider his vows’ (verse 25).

A wise king separates out the wicked like grain on the threshing floor (verse 26). “The spirit of a man is the lamp of the LORD, searching out his inmost being” (verse 27). ‘Loving devotion and faithfulness preserve a king; by these he maintains his throne’ (verse 28).

‘The glory of young men is their strength, and gray hair is the splendor of the old’ (verse 29). And the chapter ends with a saying that wounds and punishment can scour away evil (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
Verse 22 forbids personal revenge. Wait for the LORD instead. That is not passivity. It is trust that God will set things right.

Israelites could vow gifts or service to the LORD, and the law required that a vow be kept. Verse 25 warns against vowing in a rush and then having second thoughts. The story of Jephthah in Judges 11 shows how disastrous a hasty vow could be.

The king was the highest court in Israel. Verse 26 pictures him separating the wicked as a farmer separates grain from husk, driving a heavy wheel over the harvest. But verse 28 names what actually holds a throne up: not force but loving devotion and faithfulness, the covenant virtues God himself shows. Israel's history, with its many kings who fell to plots and violence, gave that saying weight.

Verse 27 pictures the human spirit as a lamp God uses to search a person's depths, the same depths verse 5 called deep waters.

Verse 30 belongs with the king's justice of verse 26. It speaks of punishment for wrongdoing in that world. It gives no one a warrant to harm anyone, and it says nothing in favor of cruelty.
passages.later: Paul repeats verse 22: ‘Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath’ (Romans 12:19). And Ecclesiastes warns about vows as verse 25 does: ‘It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it’ (Ecclesiastes 5:5).
passages.asks: The LORD directs a person's steps, and his lamp searches the heart. Ask whether there is a wrong you are waiting to pay back, and what it would mean to leave it with him. And ask what promise you have made carelessly that needs to be kept, or honestly put right.
